subject: Biology
scope: Introductory membrane transport and interpretation of model experiments; detailed electrochemical potentials are beyond this lesson.
prerequisites: Distinguish particles from the space containing them.
objectives: Explain net diffusion without attributing intention to particles.
Predict water movement through a selectively permeable membrane under stated conditions.
Distinguish passive transport from energy-dependent transport.

notes.heading: Random motion and net movement
paragraphs: Particles move randomly because of their thermal motion. If more particles are present on one side of a region, random movement initially produces more crossings away from that side than toward it. This creates net diffusion down a concentration gradient even though individual particles move in both directions. At dynamic equilibrium, motion continues but the opposing rates are equal, so there is no net change. Diffusion is faster when the gradient is steeper, the available area is larger or the diffusion distance is shorter, other conditions being equal. Higher temperature often increases particle motion, but biological systems may also change when heated.

notes.heading: Membranes and osmosis
paragraphs: A cell membrane is selectively permeable: different substances cross at different rates depending on properties such as size, charge and available transport proteins. Osmosis is net water movement through a selectively permeable membrane. For simple solutions at the same pressure with nonpenetrating solutes, water tends to move from the more dilute solution toward the more concentrated solution. More advanced descriptions use water potential because pressure also matters. A plant cell placed in sufficiently dilute surroundings can become turgid as its contents press against the cell wall. An animal cell lacks that rigid wall and may swell excessively. State the solution conditions instead of memorising a direction without context.

notes.heading: Transport proteins and experimental evidence
paragraphs: Facilitated diffusion uses membrane proteins but remains passive: net transport follows the relevant concentration or electrochemical gradient. Active transport can move substances against that gradient and requires an energy source, directly or through another coupled gradient. The presence of a protein alone therefore does not distinguish active from passive transport. To investigate water movement in tissue, compare a controlled measure such as percentage mass change, calculated relative to initial mass. Keep sample dimensions, time and temperature comparable and use repeats. A mass change supports an inference about net exchange, but does not directly show individual molecules moving or establish that every observed effect was caused by osmosis alone.

notes.heading: Interpreting experiments without confusing mechanisms
paragraphs: A change in tissue mass is an observation, not a direct measurement of every molecule crossing its membranes. In a simplified osmosis experiment, water movement can explain much of the mass change, but damaged cells, evaporation, surface liquid and dissolved substances leaving the tissue can also affect measurements. Standardise the time, temperature, starting dimensions and blotting procedure when comparing samples. Percentage mass change helps compare different starting masses, but it does not remove all differences between samples.

The concentration producing approximately zero net mass change can estimate an isotonic condition for the particular tissue and experimental conditions. It does not imply that water molecules stopped moving or that every cell has an identical internal composition. A concentration gradient can change as transport occurs, reducing the initial rate. Active transport differs because cells use energy to move selected substances against their electrochemical gradients through membrane proteins. Do not infer active transport solely from the presence of a membrane: passive diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis also involve membranes. Match the proposed mechanism to the substance, direction of movement and evidence about energy dependence.

notes.heading: Using relative mass change in an osmosis comparison
paragraphs: Compare percentage mass changes when tissue pieces begin with different masses. The denominator is the initial mass, because the question is how large the change is relative to the starting amount. A negative result indicates net mass loss, not a negative amount of tissue. In an osmosis investigation, standardise blotting before weighing so surface liquid does not masquerade as tissue water uptake. A near-zero change is consistent with little net water movement under those conditions; water molecules can still cross in both directions. Replicates, comparable tissue pieces and controlled exposure times make the comparison more interpretable. These are fictional data, not evidence that an actual investigation was performed.

workedExamples.prompt: A tissue sample increases from 2.0 g to 2.3 g. Calculate its percentage mass change.
steps: Mass change is final minus initial: 0.3 g.
Divide by initial mass and multiply by 100: 0.3/2.0×100.
Retain the positive sign to show gain.

workedExamples.prompt: Two equal-pressure solutions are separated by a membrane permeable to water but not their dissolved solute. Side A is more dilute. Predict initial net water movement.
steps: The membrane permits water exchange but prevents solute equilibration by crossing.
Under the stated simple conditions, net water movement is from the more dilute to the more concentrated solution.
Individual water molecules still move both ways.
workedExamples.answer: Initially net movement is from A toward the more concentrated side.

workedExamples.prompt: A tissue sample has no net mass change after immersion. Explain why this does not show that its membranes are impermeable to water.
steps: Net change measures the balance of movements, not the absence of movement.
Water can cross in both directions at equal average rates.
Other controls are needed to distinguish dynamic balance from a barrier that prevents movement.
workedExamples.answer: Zero net mass change is compatible with continuing water exchange.

workedExamples.prompt: In fictional tissue data, piece A changes from 2.00 g to 2.20 g and piece B from 4.00 g to 4.24 g. Calculate both percentage changes and identify the larger relative gain.
workedExamples.answer: A gains 10%; B gains 6%. A has the larger relative gain.
steps: A changes by 0.20 g, so its percentage change is 0.20/2.00 × 100 = 10%.
B changes by 0.24 g, so its percentage change is 0.24/4.00 × 100 = 6%.
Compare percentages rather than the unequal starting masses or absolute changes.

misconceptions.correction: Movement continues, but opposing rates balance.

misconceptions.claim: Every process using a membrane protein needs metabolic energy.
misconceptions.correction: Facilitated diffusion uses proteins without moving against the relevant gradient.

flashcards.front: Why say net movement in diffusion?
flashcards.back: Individual particles cross both ways; the difference between opposing rates creates the net flow.

flashcards.front: What additional condition distinguishes osmosis from ordinary diffusion in solution?
flashcards.back: Water moves through a selectively permeable membrane.

flashcards.front: What distinguishes active transport from facilitated diffusion?
flashcards.back: Active transport can move against a relevant gradient using an energy source.

flashcards.front: Why can a plant cell become turgid without immediately bursting?
flashcards.back: The cell wall resists expansion as pressure develops.

flashcards.front: Which mass is the denominator in percentage mass change?
Does zero net mass change mean no water crossed a membrane?
flashcards.back: No. It can reflect equal average movement in opposite directions.

flashcards.front: Which mass is the denominator for percentage mass change?
Does zero net water movement mean molecular motion stops?
flashcards.back: No. Movements in opposite directions can balance.

questions.prompt: A tissue sample decreases from 4.0 g to 3.6 g. Find its percentage mass change.
markingPoints: Use the signed change relative to initial mass.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes dynamic diffusion equilibrium?
options: Opposing particle movements continue at equal average rates.
Particles move only toward high concentration.
questions.answer: Opposing particle movements continue at equal average rates.
solution: Equal opposing rates produce zero net movement.

questions.prompt: Explain why the presence of a transport protein does not by itself prove active transport.
questions.answer: Proteins also mediate facilitated diffusion, which is passive. Gradient direction and energy coupling must be established.
solution: Identify facilitated diffusion as a protein-mediated passive process.
State the additional evidence needed to distinguish active transport.

questions.prompt: Two tissue samples in different solutions change mass by the same 0.2 g, but one started at 1 g and the other at 4 g. Explain why raw mass change is a poor comparison and name two controls.
questions.answer: Their percentage gains are 20% and 5%, so the relative changes differ. Comparable sample geometry, exposure time and temperature help control alternative explanations; any two are suitable.
solution: Explain that initial size affects interpretation of raw change.
markingPoints: Explain the need for relative comparison.

questions.prompt: Two groups obtain different percentage mass changes using the same solution. Propose two methodological causes and explain why repetition alone may not resolve them.
questions.answer: Different blotting procedures can leave different amounts of surface liquid, and unequal immersion times can allow different amounts of net transport. Repeating a consistently biased procedure may reproduce the same bias; standardising the method is needed as well as collecting replicates.
solution: Identify an influence on the measured mass unrelated to the intended internal water change.
Identify an uncontrolled condition affecting the transport interval.
Explain why systematic differences survive simple repetition.
markingPoints: Identify an influence on the measured mass unrelated to the intended internal water change.

questions.prompt: A learner claims that zero mass change proves water molecules stopped crossing the cell membrane. Explain the error and name one weighing control.
questions.answer: Zero net change can occur with water moving both ways at equal rates. Standardise blotting before each final mass reading.
solution: A measured total records net change, not every microscopic movement.
Consistent blotting reduces differences caused by liquid remaining on the surface.
markingPoints: A measured total records net change, not every microscopic movement.
Consistent blotting reduces differences caused by liquid remaining on the surface.

revisionChecklist: Describe random particle motion and net movement separately.
Use percentage change and controlled comparisons in evidence-based explanations.
Explain the reasoning in “Compare osmosis mass data” and correct the linked error-analysis response without copying its solution.

diagrams.title: Compare osmosis mass data
diagrams.description: Read the labelled relationships to follow this worked application. A gains 10%; B gains 6%. A has the larger relative gain. This is an explanatory process diagram, not a scale drawing or a record of a learner attempt.

steps.label: Measure consistently
steps.detail: Use the same exposure time and blotting method for each piece.

steps.label: Normalise the change
steps.detail: Divide mass change by initial mass, then multiply by 100%.

steps.label: Interpret cautiously
steps.detail: Compare net changes; do not infer that molecular movement has stopped.
